title: Did the FBI Boss Use AI to Copy a Famous Music Video?
summary: Imagine you're watching a new FBI video online, and suddenly you see shots that look just like a famous music video from 1994! That's what happened this week. FBI Director Kash Patel posted a video on X to talk about fighting fraud. But the video used the song 'Sabotage' by the Beastie Boys, and many scenes looked almost exactly like the original music video for that song. NPR found at least six clips that matched frame by frame. For example, one shot shows a car spinning out. In the original, you can see grilles in the windows, but they're missing in the FBI version. Another shot has a person jumping between roofs with telephone lines in the background. In one frame, a line goes right through the person's head—a common mistake in AI-made videos. Experts say AI was likely used to recreate the shots. 'It does seem like it would be highly likely to be AI,' said Kolina Koltai, a researcher with Bellingcat. Hany Farid, a professor at UC Berkeley, agreed. The FBI and the Beastie Boys haven't commented. Patel was a teenager when the song came out. This isn't the first time the Trump administration used pop culture in official posts, even when artists complain.
why_it_matters: It shows that even government agencies need to be careful about copying others' work, and that AI videos can be tricky to identify, so always think twice before believing what you see online.

background_read: The FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) is the main U.S. agency that investigates crimes like fraud across the country.
The Beastie Boys (a famous American hip-hop group from the 1990s) released the song 'Sabotage' in 1994; its music video is a classic.
Musicians sometimes ask politicians to stop using their songs because they don't want to be linked to political views they disagree with.
Article_Structure: WHAT: posted a video on social media that appears AI-generated, copying the 1994 'Sabotage' video
WHY: to get the public's attention about fighting fraud

perspectives.description: Using popular music and AI tricks makes a government message stand out, helping more people learn about stopping fraud.
The Beastie Boys didn't give permission, and copying their creative work without asking feels like theft.
When officials release AI‑made videos that imitate real footage, it becomes harder for the public to tell what's real and what's fake.
